# Sāleyyaka Sutta (MN 41 (PTS MN i 285))

**ID:** MN 41 (PTS MN i 285)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Sutta
**Title (Pali):** Sāleyyaka Sutta
**PTS:** MN i 285
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0201m.mul4.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Sāleyyaka Sutta* (MN 41) is the forty-first discourse of the *Majjhimanikāya*, positioned within the *Cūḷayamakavagga* [Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995; Buswell & Lopez 2014]. The discourse is set in the Kosalan brahmin village of Sālā, where the Buddha addresses a large gathering of brahmin householders (*brāhmaṇagahapatikā*) concerning the moral causes governing rebirth in favorable or unfavorable destinies [McTighe; Hazra 1994; Buswell & Lopez 2014; Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995]. The Buddha explicates the ten courses of action (*kammapatha*), contrasting unwholesome and wholesome conduct across three bodily deeds (killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct / *kāmesu micchācāra*), four verbal deeds (such as false witness in assemblies versus truthful speech), and three mental deeds (covetousness, ill will, and wrong view versus their wholesome counterparts) [Farrington; Rogell 2003; Buswell & Lopez 2014; Thanissaro Bhikkhu 2013]. He further describes how righteous conduct, combined with specific mental aspiration, leads to rebirth across twenty-five celestial planes—spanning the sense-sphere heavens (*kāmaloka*), subtle form realms (*rūpaloka*), and formless realms (*arūpaloka*)—or ultimately to liberation through the destruction of the taints [Hazra 1994; Buswell & Lopez 2014; Sagaraghosa 2011].

Within the Pali canon, the discourse is virtually identical in content to the *Verañjaka Sutta* (MN 42), which repeats its doctrinal exposition nearly verbatim for a different audience [Anālayo 2018]. The sutta is cited or referenced in canonical and paracanonical treatises including the *Niddesa* (Mnd 7, Mnd 14, Cnd 22) and the *Puggalapaññatti* (Pp 2.3). Chinese parallels are preserved in the *Saṁyuktāgama* (SĀ 1042 and SĀ 1043) [Buswell & Lopez 2014; Anālayo 2018]. Comparative study reveals that while the Pali text subdivides the Brahmā and radiant heavens (*ābhā*, *subhā*), its Chinese *Saṁyuktāgama* counterpart lists only the primary heavenly spheres, reflecting a Theravāda editorial tendency toward more elaborate cosmological taxonomies [Nattier; Anālayo 2018].

**Parallels and text reuse**

- Full parallels: MN 42 (PTS MN i 290) Verañjaka Sutta; SA 1042 鞞聞摩; SA 1043 鞞聞摩
- Passage-level parallels: AN 10.176 Cundasutta; AN 3.28 Gūthabhāṇīsutta; MN 114 (PTS MN iii 45) Sevitabbāsevitabba Sutta
- Resembling parallels: an2.6
- Mentioned in: Cnd 22 Pārāyanānugītigāthāniddesa; Mnd 14 Tuvaṭakasuttaniddesa; Mnd 7 Tissametteyyasuttaniddesa; Pp 2.3 Tikapuggalapaññatti

- [McTighe] McTighe, Mentoring in the Majjhima Nikaya — Contextual analysis of the audience as brahmin householders in Sālā

- [Anālayo 2018] Bhikkhu Anālayo, Rebirth in Early Buddhism & Current Research (2018) — Comparative analysis with MN 42 and the Saṁyuktāgama parallel regarding celestial subdivisions
